v3_contracts.title: House of Jenjie x TASCK - Service Agreement

sections.heading: Service Agreement
sections.content: This Service Agreement is dated 2026-09-02 and is made between TASCK Creative Company Limited, trading as The TASCK Agency ('TASCK'), and House of Jenjie ('Brand') for the project titled House of Jenjie - Business Call Connect. It is written to be reviewed easily before approval and signature. It explains the project scope, responsibilities, commercial terms, approval process, delivery expectations, cancellation rules, and close-out requirements.

sections.heading: 1. Parties
sections.content:
Party 1: TASCK Creative Company Limited, a registered company situated in Lagos, Nigeria.
Party 2: House of Jenjie.

TASCK and the Brand may be referred to individually as a Party and collectively as the Parties. The Parties agree to work together professionally, respond to project communications within reasonable timelines, and keep all approval decisions clear and documented.

sections.heading: 2. Background and Purpose
sections.content: The Brand has engaged TASCK to support the planning and delivery of House of Jenjie - Business Call Connect. TASCK has the strategy, creator coordination, project management, production support, and reporting capability required to deliver the approved work. The purpose of this Agreement is to record the commercial and operational terms under which TASCK will provide those services.

sections.heading: 3. Scope of Services
sections.content: TASCK will provide services that may include strategy development, creator recommendation and coordination, creative briefing, project planning, production support, content or activation oversight, performance tracking, stakeholder communication, reporting, and project close-out. The exact deliverables, dates, channels, and approval steps will follow the approved Strategy Snapshot, creator brief, deliverables schedule, and any later written amendments approved by both Parties.

sections.heading: 4. Brand Responsibilities
sections.content: The Brand will provide accurate business information, timely approvals, access to required assets, brand guidelines, payment information, stakeholder availability, and feedback needed for TASCK to deliver the project. Delays in approval, funding, asset delivery, or stakeholder response may affect timelines and may require a revised delivery schedule.

sections.heading: 5. Commercial Terms and Payment
sections.content: The total fixed fee or approved working budget for this project is ₦20,000,000. Payment will follow the approved budget and payment schedule. Unless otherwise agreed in writing, the first payment tranche is required before work begins, and any balance is due according to the agreed milestone or final delivery schedule. Work outside the approved scope, including additional creators, extra production days, usage extensions, paid media rights, venue costs, third-party services, rush delivery, or revised deliverables, must be approved in writing before TASCK proceeds.

sections.heading: 6. Project Timeline and Approvals
sections.content: The project timeline will be confirmed through the approved Strategy Snapshot, deliverables schedule, and execution plan. TASCK will submit key materials for review where approval is required. The Brand should provide consolidated feedback so the project can move efficiently. Any change in approval route, decision maker, launch date, budget, or legal requirement must be communicated to TASCK as soon as it is known.

sections.heading: 7. Performance, Reporting, and Acceptance
sections.content: TASCK will coordinate delivery and provide a final report using the information available from the approved deliverables, creator outputs, campaign performance, and project records. The Brand will review the final report and provide feedback or acceptance within a reasonable period. Once accepted, the project may be closed in TASCK.

sections.heading: 8. Intellectual Property and Usage
sections.content: Ownership and usage rights for project materials will follow the approved brief, creator contracts, paid usage terms, and any written rights schedule. TASCK does not grant rights beyond those actually secured from creators, production partners, or third parties. The Brand must not extend usage, paid media, territory, duration, exclusivity, or adaptation beyond the approved rights without written confirmation.

sections.heading: 9. Confidentiality
sections.content: Each Party will keep confidential information private, including campaign plans, commercial terms, project documents, unpublished creative, contact information, account access, strategy materials, creator negotiations, and performance data. Confidential information may only be shared with people who need it to perform the project.

sections.heading: 10. Cancellation, Delay, and Scope Changes
sections.content: If the Brand cancels, pauses, or materially changes the project after work has begun, TASCK will document the effect on schedule, cost, deliverables, third-party commitments, and creator obligations. The Brand remains responsible for approved work already completed, committed costs, cancellation charges, and reasonable time already spent. TASCK will not proceed with new or expanded work until the Parties approve the change in writing.

sections.heading: 11. Liability and Professional Conduct
sections.content: Each Party is responsible for its own negligence, misconduct, breach of confidentiality, and failure to meet documented obligations. Neither Party is responsible for delay or failure caused by events beyond reasonable control, including platform outages, government restrictions, force majeure events, third-party failure, or delayed approvals outside that Party's control.

sections.heading: 12. Governing Law and Dispute Resolution
sections.content: This Agreement is governed by the laws of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. The Parties will first attempt to resolve any dispute through good-faith discussion. If unresolved, the dispute may be referred to arbitration in accordance with applicable Nigerian arbitration law.

sections.heading: 1. Parties

sections.content:

sections.heading: 5. Fees, Expenses, and Payment
sections.content: The agreed creator fee or working budget is ₦20,000,000. Unless a separate payment schedule is agreed, payment is processed through TASCK after the required invoice, tax details, delivery confirmation, and Brand approval are received. Any production expenses, travel, third-party costs, usage extensions, exclusivity, whitelisting, or additional deliverables must be approved in writing before they are incurred. All stated fees are exclusive of applicable taxes unless clearly stated otherwise.

sections.heading: 6. Deliverables and Approval

TASCK and the Brand will review submitted work against the approved scope, not against unrelated creative preferences introduced after delivery. Reasonable revision requests may be made where the work does not match the approved brief, technical requirements, legal requirements, or brand safety standards. Additional work outside scope requires written approval before execution.

sections.heading: 7. Usage Rights and Intellectual Property
sections.content: The Creator keeps ownership of pre-existing intellectual property, likeness rights, style, methods, and materials created outside this project. Once the agreed fee is paid, the Brand receives the usage rights expressly approved in the brief or contract for the project deliverables. Broader usage, paid media extension, whitelisting, exclusivity, territory expansion, or extended duration must be agreed separately in writing.

sections.heading: 8. Confidentiality and Conduct
sections.content: The Creator, Brand, and TASCK must keep confidential information private, including unreleased campaign plans, commercial terms, internal documents, account access, talent discussions, and performance data. All parties must act professionally, avoid misleading public statements, and flag brand safety, conflict, or availability concerns immediately.

sections.heading: 9. Cancellation, Delay, and Change Control
sections.content: If the project is delayed, cancelled, or materially changed, TASCK will document the reason and confirm the effect on fees, timelines, usage, and deliverables. Work already completed, committed costs, booking commitments, and approved production costs remain payable where they cannot reasonably be recovered. Any new scope must be recorded as a written amendment before delivery continues.

sections.heading: 10. Reporting and Close-out
sections.content: After delivery, the Creator will provide reasonable supporting information needed for TASCK's final report, including live links, content files, posting dates, performance screenshots where available, and any delivery notes. TASCK will use this information to close the project accurately with the Brand.

sections.heading: 11. Governing Law and Dispute Resolution
sections.content: This Agreement is governed by the laws of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. The parties will first try to resolve any dispute through good-faith discussion. If unresolved, the dispute may be referred to arbitration in accordance with applicable Nigerian arbitration law.

sections.heading: Independent Creator Agreement
sections.content: This Independent Creator Agreement is dated 2026-09-03 and is made for the project titled PLUTO Verifyme.NG - Business Call Connect. It records the working relationship between Adesuwa Etomi Wellington, PLUTO Verifyme.NG, and TASCK Creative Company Limited, trading operationally as The TASCK Agency. The document is written for clear review before signature: it explains the creator role, the brand responsibilities, TASCK's coordination role, the fee basis, approval process, usage rights, reporting expectations, and the signature requirements.

sections.heading: 1. Parties
sections.content:
Creator: Adesuwa Etomi Wellington.
Brand: PLUTO Verifyme.NG.
Agency / coordinator: TASCK Creative Company Limited, trading as The TASCK Agency.

The Creator is engaged as an independent creative partner. Nothing in this Agreement creates an employment relationship, partnership, or exclusive agency relationship unless the parties agree to that separately in writing.

sections.heading: 2. Project Reference
sections.content:
Project title: PLUTO Verifyme.NG - Business Call Connect.
Contract value / creator fee basis: ₦250,000.
The final scope, dates, deliverables, approvals, and usage terms must match the approved Strategy Snapshot, creator brief, and any later written amendments approved by TASCK and the Brand.

sections.heading: 3. Creator Responsibilities
sections.content: The Creator will contribute creative thinking, audience understanding, content direction, appearances, production input, and/or delivery support as agreed in the approved brief. The Creator must communicate availability, production requirements, usage limits, fee assumptions, and any restrictions that may affect delivery before work begins. The Creator will deliver work professionally, on time, and in a format suitable for Brand and TASCK review.

sections.heading: 4. TASCK Responsibilities
sections.content: TASCK will coordinate communication between the Brand and the Creator, issue or manage the approved brief, support production administration, track approvals, manage reporting, and administer payment in line with the agreed commercial terms. TASCK does not take over the Creator's creative voice; TASCK helps make the agreed project executable, documented, and accountable.

sections.heading: 5. Fees, Expenses, and Payment
sections.content: The agreed creator fee or working budget is ₦250,000. Unless a separate payment schedule is agreed, payment is processed through TASCK after the required invoice, tax details, delivery confirmation, and Brand approval are received. Any production expenses, travel, third-party costs, usage extensions, exclusivity, whitelisting, or additional deliverables must be approved in writing before they are incurred. All stated fees are exclusive of applicable taxes unless clearly stated otherwise.

sections.heading: 6. Deliverables and Approval
sections.content: Deliverables must follow the approved creator brief and execution schedule. TASCK and the Brand will review submitted work against the approved scope, not against unrelated creative preferences introduced after delivery. Reasonable revision requests may be made where the work does not match the approved brief, technical requirements, legal requirements, or brand safety standards. Additional work outside scope requires written approval before execution.

sections.heading: 7. Usage Rights and Intellectual Property
sections.content: The Creator keeps ownership of pre-existing intellectual property, likeness rights, style, methods, and materials created outside this project. Once the agreed fee is paid, the Brand receives the usage rights expressly approved in the brief or contract for the project deliverables. Broader usage, paid media extension, whitelisting, exclusivity, territory expansion, or extended duration must be agreed separately in writing.

sections.heading: 8. Confidentiality and Conduct
sections.content: The Creator, Brand, and TASCK must keep confidential information private, including unreleased campaign plans, commercial terms, internal documents, account access, talent discussions, and performance data. All parties must act professionally, avoid misleading public statements, and flag brand safety, conflict, or availability concerns immediately.

sections.heading: 9. Cancellation, Delay, and Change Control
sections.content: If the project is delayed, cancelled, or materially changed, TASCK will document the reason and confirm the effect on fees, timelines, usage, and deliverables. Work already completed, committed costs, booking commitments, and approved production costs remain payable where they cannot reasonably be recovered. Any new scope must be recorded as a written amendment before delivery continues.

sections.heading: 10. Reporting and Close-out
sections.content: After delivery, the Creator will provide reasonable supporting information needed for TASCK's final report, including live links, content files, posting dates, performance screenshots where available, and any delivery notes. TASCK will use this information to close the project accurately with the Brand.

sections.heading: 11. Governing Law and Dispute Resolution
sections.content: This Agreement is governed by the laws of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. The parties will first try to resolve any dispute through good-faith discussion. If unresolved, the dispute may be referred to arbitration in accordance with applicable Nigerian arbitration law.

v3_email_outbox.body:
Hello Ifedayo Agoro,

Welcome to TASCK. A new creator brief is ready for your review.

Business Case: House of Jenjie - Business Call Connect
Creator Portal: https://thcodemo.space/creator
Username: ifedayo@thetasck.com
Access code: TASCK-DCE2-6F5C

Please log in, review the brief, and respond with your interest, fee expectation, conditions, and availability.

Creative Brief:
CREATOR ROLE BRIEF: HOUSE OF JENJIE - BUSINESS CALL CONNECT
Duration: October - December 2026
Prepared for: Ifedayo Agoro

The Opportunity:
House of Jenjie is a premium Nigerian herbal tea brand launching caffeine-free wellness blends that reposition local tea from traditional medicine to world-class lifestyle products. The brand sits alongside Pukka and Lipton, crafted for consumers who curate health-conscious choices without compromising on quality or taste.
This matters to your audience because they are actively seeking premium wellness options that align with their lifestyle values:
- Caffeine-free herbal wellness blends
- Premium Nigerian ingredients repositioned globally
- Lifestyle product not medicinal remedy
- Available at trusted supermarket retailers
- World-class quality meets local heritage

Your Role:
You are House of Jenjie's Wellness Lifestyle Ambassador, the trusted voice that introduces premium Nigerian tea as a daily ritual for health-conscious consumers who shop with intention. You embody the shift from 'what does it cure?' to 'how does it elevate my day?'.
This shows up as authentic integration into your wellness routines, shopping hauls from premium retailers, and conversations that position House of Jenjie as part of a curated lifestyle your audience already aspires to live.

Core Narrative (Non-Negotiable):
All content must reinforce one clear story:
Nigerian herbal tea is no longer medicine - it is premium wellness your lifestyle deserves.
Your content should bring these four pillars to life:
- Premium Repositioning - local ingredients meet world-class standards
- Lifestyle Integration - daily rituals not occasional remedies
- Retail Visibility - supermarket presence builds trust and accessibility
- Health-Conscious Choice - caffeine-free wellness for mindful consumers

What You'll Do:
1. Brand Introduction and Positioning
- Launch content introducing House of Jenjie
- Highlight premium quality and caffeine-free benefits
- Position alongside global wellness tea brands
2. Lifestyle Integration Content
- Show tea in daily wellness routines
- Create aspirational lifestyle moments with product
- Demonstrate versatility beyond traditional tea consumption
3. Retail Awareness and Call-to-Action
- Feature supermarket shopping content with House of Jenjie
- Direct audiences to specific retail stockists
- Include digital purchase links for online delivery
4. Community Engagement and Conversion
- Host wellness conversations around premium Nigerian products
- Engage followers on health-conscious lifestyle choices
- Drive awareness that converts to purchase intent

Content Approach:
Content is not one-off, it is a series designed to:
- Reposition Nigerian tea as premium lifestyle
- Drive supermarket awareness and product trial
- Convert online engagement to offline sales
- Build brand credibility through authentic integration
Your creativity is key, but every piece of content should move your audience to act.

Creator Benefits (Limited Access):
- Three-month ambassador partnership fee
- Performance-based commercial incentives tied to sales
- Product supply for personal use
- First-mover positioning with emerging premium brand
- Long-term partnership potential beyond initial activation
- Brand collaboration content for portfolio
- Access to House of Jenjie events
- Priority consideration for future brand campaigns

Success Metrics:
- Five thousand to fifteen thousand sales
- Five million total audience reach
- Retail stockist awareness and inquiries
- Online-to-offline conversion through purchase links
- Sustained engagement on wellness lifestyle content

Commercial Model:
Hybrid structure:
- Fixed base fee
- Performance-based incentives (approx. 50%) tied to:
  - Sales milestones per tea boxes
  - Retail pull-through from target supermarkets
  - Documented conversion via tracked links
  - Audience reach and engagement thresholds

Next Steps:
Ifedayo Agoro, if you're interested, reply with your rate card or let us know a good time to connect - we'll take it from there.

alignment_snapshot_fields.about_the_organisation: Nike operates in the sportswear and athletic footwear category, focusing on Nigeria as a key growth market. The brand already commands strong awareness and aspiration among Nigerian consumers, many of whom purchase Nike products for fashion and cultural capital rather than active participation in sport. The immediate commercial challenge is not building brand recognition but converting brand admiration into sustained athletic behaviour - specifically, growing participation in running. The marketing team has identified a gap between product purchase and community engagement: while Nike enjoys robust sales, participation in organised runs, local running clubs, and weekend fitness groups remains relatively small. Previous influencer campaigns have generated reach, engagement, video views, and short-term sales lift, but have not built lasting communities or sustained participation beyond campaign windows. The brand seeks to shift from advertising-led growth to community-led behaviour change, designing ecosystems that reduce emotional barriers to participation and make running socially desirable. This strategic pivot reflects a recognition that Nigerian audiences require authenticity and locally-created experiences rather than localised adaptations of global assets.
alignment_snapshot_fields.core_focus_areas: The primary focus is driving active participation in running, not simply promoting product ownership. The brand is exploring creator-led community strategies as an alternative to traditional influencer marketing, with creators positioned as community builders rather than content distributors. The organisation is evaluating how to design ecosystems that include running clubs, creator stories, music, weekly participation challenges, digital content, and community identity markers. There is a deliberate effort to move from campaign-based thinking to sustained community infrastructure, where content serves as evidence that the community exists rather than the primary driver of engagement. Authenticity and local cultural relevance are critical priorities, with the marketing team explicitly seeking to avoid imported campaigns that do not resonate with Nigerian cultural norms and social behaviours.
alignment_snapshot_fields.key_customers_beneficiaries: The primary audience comprises Nigerian consumers who already know and aspire to own Nike products but have not yet adopted running as a regular behaviour. This includes fashion-conscious buyers who purchase Nike for cultural reasons but do not participate in organised fitness activities. The opportunity lies with potential runners who face emotional and social barriers to participation - people who may be interested in running but lack the community invitation or social permission to begin. The brand is particularly interested in reaching audiences through community creators who already have trust and influence within local running groups, weekend fitness communities, and neighbourhood networks. The target is not mass awareness but behaviour conversion: moving individuals from passive brand appreciation to active athletic participation through trusted peer networks and locally-rooted community structures.
alignment_snapshot_fields.key_goals_metrics: The organisation currently measures marketing performance primarily through media metrics including reach, engagement, video views, traffic, and sales during campaign windows. The marketing team has acknowledged that they lack a structured framework to measure participation itself - a gap they recognise as limiting their ability to assess behaviour change campaigns effectively. The stated ambition is to shift measurement focus from impressions and short-term sales lift to sustained participation in running communities, community membership growth, and repeat engagement with running activities. The brand is seeking to develop new metrics that track identity formation, belonging, and behaviour adoption rather than media consumption alone. Previous campaigns have delivered strong reach and engagement but have struggled to sustain momentum after campaigns finish, indicating a need for measurement systems that assess long-term community health and ongoing participation rather than one-off activation success.
alignment_snapshot_fields.success_timeline: The engagement is structured as a phased approach beginning with discovery and alignment before moving to strategy development. The brand has committed to sharing audience research, previous campaign performance data, and current business priorities to enable proper diagnostic work. The immediate next step involves preparing an Alignment Snapshot to ensure shared understanding of the opportunity before any solutions are recommended. Following alignment, the planned deliverables include an initial creator strategy, recommended creator archetypes, a participation measurement framework, and a strategic workshop to define the ecosystem design. The timeline reflects a deliberate choice to avoid jumping directly into tactical execution, prioritising strategic clarity and evidence-based planning. The brand has indicated willingness to move through a structured process that begins with understanding existing data and performance before committing to specific community-building initiatives or creator partnerships.
alignment_snapshot_fields.focus: The strategic focus is shifting from reach optimisation to behaviour change, with community building positioned as the primary mechanism for growth. The brand is moving away from influencer campaigns designed purely for content distribution toward creator partnerships where creators are accountable for building and sustaining communities. The emphasis is on creating social permission and reducing emotional barriers to participation, rather than simply promoting product features or aspirational messaging. There is a strong preference for locally-created experiences that feel genuinely Nigerian rather than localised versions of global campaigns. The organisation is exploring a hybrid model that combines celebrity creators for attention with community creators for sustained participation, recognising that different creator archetypes serve different strategic roles. The focus is on designing ecosystems where running clubs, challenges, music, and digital content work together to create community identity and normalise running as a social behaviour.
alignment_snapshot_fields.priority: The highest priority is converting brand awareness into active participation in running, addressing the gap between product purchase and athletic behaviour. The brand is prioritising authenticity and local cultural resonance over global campaign adaptation, seeking creators and community structures that feel native to Nigerian audiences. There is a clear priority to move beyond short-term campaign windows toward sustained community infrastructure that continues to drive participation after initial activations end. The marketing team is prioritising the development of new measurement frameworks that assess participation and behaviour change rather than relying solely on traditional media metrics. Strategic clarity is prioritised over immediate execution, with the brand committed to completing diagnostic work and alignment before committing to specific tactics. The organisation is also prioritising the shift from advertising thinking to community-builder thinking, recognising this as a fundamental strategic reorientation rather than a tactical adjustment to existing campaign models.

--- Transcript ---
Nike x TTA: Exploring Creator-Led Growth for Nike Running - March 12
VIEW RECORDING – 58 mins (No highlights)

@0:00 – Sarah Johnson (Nike Marketing Director)
Jude, thank you for making the time. We've been following some of the work you've been doing around creator communities and behaviour change, and we thought this would be a good opportunity to exchange ideas.
To give a little context, we're currently looking closely at how we grow participation in running across Nigeria.
Nike is already a very well-known brand here, but awareness isn't really our challenge anymore.
The bigger question for us is how we move people from admiring the brand to actually putting on running shoes and becoming runners.
That's really the conversation we'd like to have today.

@1:38 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's really interesting because I actually think you've just described a behaviour problem rather than a marketing problem.
People already know Nike.
They probably even aspire to own Nike.
But becoming a runner is something completely different.
From our perspective, behaviour usually changes through trusted communities much faster than it changes through advertising.
So I don't think the question becomes "How do we advertise running?"
I think the question becomes "Who already has permission to influence that behaviour?"

@3:02 – Michael Adeyemi (Nike Brand Manager)
Exactly.
One thing we've observed is that many people buy Nike because it's fashionable.
But when we look at participation in organised runs, local running clubs or even weekend fitness groups, the numbers are still relatively small.
We think there's an opportunity there.
We've experimented with influencer campaigns before.
They've generated reach.
They've generated engagement.
But they haven't necessarily built communities.

@5:11 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Can I ask something?
When you evaluate those influencer campaigns internally, are you primarily measuring media metrics?
Or are you measuring behaviour?
Because those are very different things.
If you're looking at impressions, influencers perform one role.
If you're trying to create identity and belonging, the strategy changes completely.

@6:25 – Ada Obi (Nike Digital Marketing Lead)
Mostly media metrics.
Reach.
Engagement.
Video views.
Traffic.
Sales during campaign windows.
We've never really had a structured way to measure participation itself.

@7:42 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's helpful.
One thing we've learned is that creators become much more valuable when they're responsible for building communities rather than distributing content.
Someone doesn't wake up and become a runner because they watched one video.
They become runners because someone invited them into a community where running became normal.

@10:18 – Sarah Johnson
That's actually one of the reasons we're interested in this conversation.
We've started asking ourselves whether we should think less like advertisers and more like community builders.

@12:05 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
I think that's exactly where creators become strategic partners.
The creator isn't simply promoting the shoe.
They're making the behaviour socially desirable.
They're reducing the emotional barriers to participation.

@15:14 – Michael Adeyemi
One thing we'd like to avoid is another campaign that feels imported.
We've got incredible global assets, but Nigerian audiences respond differently.
We need something that genuinely feels local.

@17:20 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's actually encouraging to hear because authenticity is probably the biggest predictor of success for creator-led campaigns.
People can tell almost immediately when something has simply been localized versus genuinely created for them.

@21:11 – Sarah Johnson
Another question we'd love your thoughts on.
Should we work with celebrities?
Or should we work with smaller creators who already run communities?

@22:35 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Personally...
I don't think that's an either-or question.
Celebrities create attention.
Community creators create participation.
If the objective is behaviour change, I'd expect the community layer to carry much more weight.

@28:42 – Ada Obi
That's interesting because internally we've tended to optimise for reach.
Maybe that's why we've struggled to sustain momentum after campaigns finish.

@33:15 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Exactly.
What we're really designing isn't a campaign.
We're designing an ecosystem.
Running clubs.
Creator stories.
Music.
Weekly participation.
Challenges.
Digital content.
Community identity.
The content becomes evidence that the community exists—not the other way around.

@41:56 – Sarah Johnson
I think that's a useful distinction.
This feels much closer to what we're actually trying to achieve.

@46:18 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
I don't think we'd want to jump straight into solutions today.
Our next step should really be understanding your existing audience data, previous campaign performance and business priorities.
Once we understand that properly, we'll prepare an Alignment Snapshot to make sure we've understood the opportunity before recommending anything.

@51:02 – Sarah Johnson
That sounds like a sensible approach.
We'll share our audience insights, previous campaign summaries and current priorities over the next week.

ACTION ITEMS
Nike
Share audience research.
Share previous campaign performance.
Share priority product categories.
Introduce regional marketing stakeholders.
TTA
Prepare Alignment Snapshot.
Develop initial creator strategy.
Recommend creator archetypes.
Prepare measurement framework.
Schedule strategic workshop.

@0:00 – Sarah Johnson (Nike Marketing Director)
Jude, thank you for making the time. We've been following some of the work you've been doing around creator communities and behaviour change, and we thought this would be a good opportunity to exchange ideas.
To give a little context, we're currently looking closely at how we grow participation in running across Nigeria.
Nike is already a very well-known brand here, but awareness isn't really our challenge anymore.
The bigger question for us is how we move people from admiring the brand to actually putting on running shoes and becoming runners.
That's really the conversation we'd like to have today.

@1:38 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's really interesting because I actually think you've just described a behaviour problem rather than a marketing problem.
People already know Nike.
They probably even aspire to own Nike.
But becoming a runner is something completely different.
From our perspective, behaviour usually changes through trusted communities much faster than it changes through advertising.
So I don't think the question becomes "How do we advertise running?"
I think the question becomes "Who already has permission to influence that behaviour?"

@3:02 – Michael Adeyemi (Nike Brand Manager)
Exactly.
One thing we've observed is that many people buy Nike because it's fashionable.
But when we look at participation in organised runs, local running clubs or even weekend fitness groups, the numbers are still relatively small.
We think there's an opportunity there.
We've experimented with influencer campaigns before.
They've generated reach.
They've generated engagement.
But they haven't necessarily built communities.

@5:11 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Can I ask something?
When you evaluate those influencer campaigns internally, are you primarily measuring media metrics?
Or are you measuring behaviour?
Because those are very different things.
If you're looking at impressions, influencers perform one role.
If you're trying to create identity and belonging, the strategy changes completely.

@6:25 – Ada Obi (Nike Digital Marketing Lead)
Mostly media metrics.
Reach.
Engagement.
Video views.
Traffic.
Sales during campaign windows.
We've never really had a structured way to measure participation itself.

@7:42 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's helpful.
One thing we've learned is that creators become much more valuable when they're responsible for building communities rather than distributing content.
Someone doesn't wake up and become a runner because they watched one video.
They become runners because someone invited them into a community where running became normal.

@10:18 – Sarah Johnson

@12:05 – Jude Abaga (TTA)

@28:42 – Ada Obi

@33:15 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Exactly.

alignment_tool_analysis.about_the_organisation: Nike operates in the sportswear and athletic footwear category, focusing on Nigeria as a key growth market. The brand already commands strong awareness and aspiration among Nigerian consumers, many of whom purchase Nike products for fashion and cultural capital rather than active participation in sport. The immediate commercial challenge is not building brand recognition but converting brand admiration into sustained athletic behaviour - specifically, growing participation in running. The marketing team has identified a gap between product purchase and community engagement: while Nike enjoys robust sales, participation in organised runs, local running clubs, and weekend fitness groups remains relatively small. Previous influencer campaigns have generated reach, engagement, video views, and short-term sales lift, but have not built lasting communities or sustained participation beyond campaign windows. The brand seeks to shift from advertising-led growth to community-led behaviour change, designing ecosystems that reduce emotional barriers to participation and make running socially desirable. This strategic pivot reflects a recognition that Nigerian audiences require authenticity and locally-created experiences rather than localised adaptations of global assets.
alignment_tool_analysis.core_focus_areas: The primary focus is driving active participation in running, not simply promoting product ownership. The brand is exploring creator-led community strategies as an alternative to traditional influencer marketing, with creators positioned as community builders rather than content distributors. The organisation is evaluating how to design ecosystems that include running clubs, creator stories, music, weekly participation challenges, digital content, and community identity markers. There is a deliberate effort to move from campaign-based thinking to sustained community infrastructure, where content serves as evidence that the community exists rather than the primary driver of engagement. Authenticity and local cultural relevance are critical priorities, with the marketing team explicitly seeking to avoid imported campaigns that do not resonate with Nigerian cultural norms and social behaviours.
alignment_tool_analysis.key_customers_beneficiaries: The primary audience comprises Nigerian consumers who already know and aspire to own Nike products but have not yet adopted running as a regular behaviour. This includes fashion-conscious buyers who purchase Nike for cultural reasons but do not participate in organised fitness activities. The opportunity lies with potential runners who face emotional and social barriers to participation - people who may be interested in running but lack the community invitation or social permission to begin. The brand is particularly interested in reaching audiences through community creators who already have trust and influence within local running groups, weekend fitness communities, and neighbourhood networks. The target is not mass awareness but behaviour conversion: moving individuals from passive brand appreciation to active athletic participation through trusted peer networks and locally-rooted community structures.
alignment_tool_analysis.key_goals_metrics: The organisation currently measures marketing performance primarily through media metrics including reach, engagement, video views, traffic, and sales during campaign windows. The marketing team has acknowledged that they lack a structured framework to measure participation itself - a gap they recognise as limiting their ability to assess behaviour change campaigns effectively. The stated ambition is to shift measurement focus from impressions and short-term sales lift to sustained participation in running communities, community membership growth, and repeat engagement with running activities. The brand is seeking to develop new metrics that track identity formation, belonging, and behaviour adoption rather than media consumption alone. Previous campaigns have delivered strong reach and engagement but have struggled to sustain momentum after campaigns finish, indicating a need for measurement systems that assess long-term community health and ongoing participation rather than one-off activation success.
alignment_tool_analysis.success_timeline: The engagement is structured as a phased approach beginning with discovery and alignment before moving to strategy development. The brand has committed to sharing audience research, previous campaign performance data, and current business priorities to enable proper diagnostic work. The immediate next step involves preparing an Alignment Snapshot to ensure shared understanding of the opportunity before any solutions are recommended. Following alignment, the planned deliverables include an initial creator strategy, recommended creator archetypes, a participation measurement framework, and a strategic workshop to define the ecosystem design. The timeline reflects a deliberate choice to avoid jumping directly into tactical execution, prioritising strategic clarity and evidence-based planning. The brand has indicated willingness to move through a structured process that begins with understanding existing data and performance before committing to specific community-building initiatives or creator partnerships.
alignment_tool_analysis.focus: The strategic focus is shifting from reach optimisation to behaviour change, with community building positioned as the primary mechanism for growth. The brand is moving away from influencer campaigns designed purely for content distribution toward creator partnerships where creators are accountable for building and sustaining communities. The emphasis is on creating social permission and reducing emotional barriers to participation, rather than simply promoting product features or aspirational messaging. There is a strong preference for locally-created experiences that feel genuinely Nigerian rather than localised versions of global campaigns. The organisation is exploring a hybrid model that combines celebrity creators for attention with community creators for sustained participation, recognising that different creator archetypes serve different strategic roles. The focus is on designing ecosystems where running clubs, challenges, music, and digital content work together to create community identity and normalise running as a social behaviour.
alignment_tool_analysis.priority: The highest priority is converting brand awareness into active participation in running, addressing the gap between product purchase and athletic behaviour. The brand is prioritising authenticity and local cultural resonance over global campaign adaptation, seeking creators and community structures that feel native to Nigerian audiences. There is a clear priority to move beyond short-term campaign windows toward sustained community infrastructure that continues to drive participation after initial activations end. The marketing team is prioritising the development of new measurement frameworks that assess participation and behaviour change rather than relying solely on traditional media metrics. Strategic clarity is prioritised over immediate execution, with the brand committed to completing diagnostic work and alignment before committing to specific tactics. The organisation is also prioritising the shift from advertising thinking to community-builder thinking, recognising this as a fundamental strategic reorientation rather than a tactical adjustment to existing campaign models.

alignment_snapshot_fields.about_the_organisation: Nike Inc operates in Nigeria as a globally recognised sportswear and athletic footwear brand within the tech-enabled consumer fitness sector. The organisation enjoys strong brand awareness and aspirational appeal across Nigerian markets, particularly for its running category products. Despite widespread recognition and fashion-driven purchase behaviour, the brand faces a strategic challenge in converting brand admiration into active participation in running. The marketing team has identified a gap between consumer ownership of Nike products and actual engagement in organised fitness activities such as local running clubs, weekend fitness groups, and structured running events. Previous influencer-led campaigns have delivered strong media metrics including reach, engagement, video views, and traffic during campaign windows, but have not sustained momentum or built lasting communities around running participation. The brand is now exploring a shift from traditional advertising approaches toward community-building strategies that address behaviour change rather than awareness. This reorientation reflects a recognition that Nigerian audiences require locally authentic engagement rather than imported campaign models, and that participation in running as a lifestyle behaviour requires different metrics and creator partnerships than product promotion alone.
alignment_snapshot_fields.core_focus_areas: The organisation is focused on growing participation in running across Nigeria, moving beyond brand awareness to drive actual behaviour change among consumers who already know and admire the brand. The marketing leadership is investigating how creator-led community strategies can transition consumers from product ownership to active running participation. This includes examining the distinction between media-optimised influencer campaigns and community-centred creator partnerships that foster identity and belonging around running. The brand is also prioritising authenticity and local resonance over globalised campaign templates, acknowledging that Nigerian audiences require engagement strategies that feel genuinely created for them rather than simply localised.
alignment_snapshot_fields.key_customers_beneficiaries: The primary audience comprises Nigerian consumers who currently purchase Nike products for fashion reasons but have not yet adopted running as a regular behaviour or lifestyle practice. This audience demonstrates strong brand affinity and ownership intent but shows limited participation in organised running activities, local running clubs, or weekend fitness groups. The brand recognises that these consumers require social permission and community invitation to transition from product buyers to active runners. The marketing team has observed that this audience responds differently to imported campaign models and requires locally authentic engagement to reduce emotional barriers to participation in running.
alignment_snapshot_fields.key_goals_metrics: The organisation's central objective is to increase participation in running as a measurable behaviour rather than optimising traditional media metrics. Historically, the brand has evaluated campaigns primarily through reach, engagement, video views, traffic, and sales during campaign windows, but acknowledges it lacks a structured framework to measure participation itself. The marketing team is now seeking to establish metrics around community formation, sustained momentum beyond campaign periods, and ongoing engagement in running clubs, fitness groups, and organised running events. Success will be measured by whether consumers transition from admiring the brand to consistently putting on running shoes and identifying as runners within community structures.
alignment_snapshot_fields.success_timeline: The organisation is approaching this strategic shift as a foundational reorientation rather than a short-term campaign, acknowledging that behaviour change requires ecosystem development rather than discrete activation windows. The brand has committed to sharing audience research, previous campaign performance data, and current priorities to inform strategy development. The marketing leadership recognises that sustaining momentum beyond traditional campaign cycles has been a previous weakness and that building communities around running participation will require longer-term investment in creator partnerships, running clubs, weekly participation structures, and community identity development rather than burst-based media spending.
alignment_snapshot_fields.focus: The brand's strategic focus centres on reframing its marketing challenge from an awareness problem to a behaviour change problem, recognising that consumers already know Nike but require trusted communities and social permission to become active runners. The organisation is investigating how creators can function as community builders rather than content distributors, making running socially desirable and reducing emotional barriers to participation. This includes exploring the distinction between celebrity partnerships that generate attention and community creators who drive participation, with an expectation that community-layer creators will carry greater weight if behaviour change is the true objective. The marketing team is also examining how to design ecosystems that integrate running clubs, creator stories, music, weekly participation structures, challenges, digital content, and community identity rather than isolated campaign assets.
alignment_snapshot_fields.priority: The organisation's immediate priority is to understand the full scope of its existing audience data, previous campaign performance across media and behavioural dimensions, and internal business priorities before committing to strategic recommendations. The brand has identified a need to develop new measurement frameworks that capture participation rather than impressions, and to establish creator partnership models that prioritise authenticity and community formation over reach optimisation. The marketing leadership is also prioritising the development of locally authentic engagement strategies that feel genuinely Nigerian rather than adapted from global templates, acknowledging that this authenticity is a critical predictor of success for creator-led campaigns. The team is preparing to introduce regional marketing stakeholders and receive strategic recommendations including creator archetypes, initial creator strategy, and measurement frameworks that align with behaviour change objectives.

--- Transcript ---
Nike x TTA: Exploring Creator-Led Growth for Nike Running - March 12
VIEW RECORDING – 58 mins (No highlights)

@0:00 – Sarah Johnson (Nike Marketing Director)
Jude, thank you for making the time. We've been following some of the work you've been doing around creator communities and behaviour change, and we thought this would be a good opportunity to exchange ideas.
To give a little context, we're currently looking closely at how we grow participation in running across Nigeria.
Nike is already a very well-known brand here, but awareness isn't really our challenge anymore.
The bigger question for us is how we move people from admiring the brand to actually putting on running shoes and becoming runners.
That's really the conversation we'd like to have today.

@1:38 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's really interesting because I actually think you've just described a behaviour problem rather than a marketing problem.
People already know Nike.
They probably even aspire to own Nike.
But becoming a runner is something completely different.
From our perspective, behaviour usually changes through trusted communities much faster than it changes through advertising.
So I don't think the question becomes "How do we advertise running?"
I think the question becomes "Who already has permission to influence that behaviour?"

@3:02 – Michael Adeyemi (Nike Brand Manager)
Exactly.
One thing we've observed is that many people buy Nike because it's fashionable.
But when we look at participation in organised runs, local running clubs or even weekend fitness groups, the numbers are still relatively small.
We think there's an opportunity there.
We've experimented with influencer campaigns before.
They've generated reach.
They've generated engagement.
But they haven't necessarily built communities.

@5:11 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Can I ask something?
When you evaluate those influencer campaigns internally, are you primarily measuring media metrics?
Or are you measuring behaviour?
Because those are very different things.
If you're looking at impressions, influencers perform one role.
If you're trying to create identity and belonging, the strategy changes completely.

@6:25 – Ada Obi (Nike Digital Marketing Lead)
Mostly media metrics.
Reach.
Engagement.
Video views.
Traffic.
Sales during campaign windows.
We've never really had a structured way to measure participation itself.

@7:42 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's helpful.
One thing we've learned is that creators become much more valuable when they're responsible for building communities rather than distributing content.
Someone doesn't wake up and become a runner because they watched one video.
They become runners because someone invited them into a community where running became normal.

@10:18 – Sarah Johnson
That's actually one of the reasons we're interested in this conversation.
We've started asking ourselves whether we should think less like advertisers and more like community builders.

@12:05 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
I think that's exactly where creators become strategic partners.
The creator isn't simply promoting the shoe.
They're making the behaviour socially desirable.
They're reducing the emotional barriers to participation.

@15:14 – Michael Adeyemi
One thing we'd like to avoid is another campaign that feels imported.
We've got incredible global assets, but Nigerian audiences respond differently.
We need something that genuinely feels local.

@17:20 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's actually encouraging to hear because authenticity is probably the biggest predictor of success for creator-led campaigns.
People can tell almost immediately when something has simply been localized versus genuinely created for them.

@21:11 – Sarah Johnson
Another question we'd love your thoughts on.
Should we work with celebrities?
Or should we work with smaller creators who already run communities?

@22:35 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Personally...
I don't think that's an either-or question.
Celebrities create attention.
Community creators create participation.
If the objective is behaviour change, I'd expect the community layer to carry much more weight.

@28:42 – Ada Obi
That's interesting because internally we've tended to optimise for reach.
Maybe that's why we've struggled to sustain momentum after campaigns finish.

@33:15 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Exactly.
What we're really designing isn't a campaign.
We're designing an ecosystem.
Running clubs.
Creator stories.
Music.
Weekly participation.
Challenges.
Digital content.
Community identity.
The content becomes evidence that the community exists—not the other way around.

@41:56 – Sarah Johnson
I think that's a useful distinction.
This feels much closer to what we're actually trying to achieve.

@46:18 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
I don't think we'd want to jump straight into solutions today.
Our next step should really be understanding your existing audience data, previous campaign performance and business priorities.
Once we understand that properly, we'll prepare an Alignment Snapshot to make sure we've understood the opportunity before recommending anything.

@51:02 – Sarah Johnson
That sounds like a sensible approach.

VIEW RECORDING – 58 mins (No highlights)

@0:00 – Sarah Johnson (Nike Marketing Director)
Jude, thank you for making the time. We've been following some of the work you've been doing around creator communities and behaviour change, and we thought this would be a good opportunity to exchange ideas.
To give a little context, we're currently looking closely at how we grow participation in running across Nigeria.
Nike is already a very well-known brand here, but awareness isn't really our challenge anymore.
The bigger question for us is how we move people from admiring the brand to actually putting on running shoes and becoming runners.
That's really the conversation we'd like to have today.

@1:38 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's really interesting because I actually think you've just described a behaviour problem rather than a marketing problem.
People already know Nike.
They probably even aspire to own Nike.
But becoming a runner is something completely different.
From our perspective, behaviour usually changes through trusted communities much faster than it changes through advertising.
So I don't think the question becomes "How do we advertise running?"
I think the question becomes "Who already has permission to influence that behaviour?"

@3:02 – Michael Adeyemi (Nike Brand Manager)
Exactly.
One thing we've observed is that many people buy Nike because it's fashionable.
But when we look at participation in organised runs, local running clubs or even weekend fitness groups, the numbers are still relatively small.
We think there's an opportunity there.
We've experimented with influencer campaigns before.
They've generated reach.
They've generated engagement.
But they haven't necessarily built communities.

@5:11 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Can I ask something?
When you evaluate those influencer campaigns internally, are you primarily measuring media metrics?
Or are you measuring behaviour?
Because those are very different things.
If you're looking at impressions, influencers perform one role.
If you're trying to create identity and belonging, the strategy changes completely.

@6:25 – Ada Obi (Nike Digital Marketing Lead)
Mostly media metrics.
Reach.
Engagement.
Video views.
Traffic.
Sales during campaign windows.
We've never really had a structured way to measure participation itself.

@7:42 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's helpful.
One thing we've learned is that creators become much more valuable when they're responsible for building communities rather than distributing content.
Someone doesn't wake up and become a runner because they watched one video.
They become runners because someone invited them into a community where running became normal.

@10:18 – Sarah Johnson
That's actually one of the reasons we're interested in this conversation.
We've started asking ourselves whether we should think less like advertisers and more like community builders.

@12:05 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
I think that's exactly where creators become strategic partners.
The creator isn't simply promoting the shoe.
They're making the behaviour socially desirable.
They're reducing the emotional barriers to participation.

@15:14 – Michael Adeyemi
One thing we'd like to avoid is another campaign that feels imported.
We've got incredible global assets, but Nigerian audiences respond differently.
We need something that genuinely feels local.

@17:20 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's actually encouraging to hear because authenticity is probably the biggest predictor of success for creator-led campaigns.
People can tell almost immediately when something has simply been localized versus genuinely created for them.

@21:11 – Sarah Johnson
Another question we'd love your thoughts on.
Should we work with celebrities?
Or should we work with smaller creators who already run communities?

@22:35 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Personally...
I don't think that's an either-or question.
Celebrities create attention.
Community creators create participation.
If the objective is behaviour change, I'd expect the community layer to carry much more weight.

@28:42 – Ada Obi
That's interesting because internally we've tended to optimise for reach.
Maybe that's why we've struggled to sustain momentum after campaigns finish.

@33:15 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Exactly.
What we're really designing isn't a campaign.
We're designing an ecosystem.
Running clubs.
Creator stories.
Music.
Weekly participation.
Challenges.
Digital content.
Community identity.
The content becomes evidence that the community exists—not the other way around.

@41:56 – Sarah Johnson
I think that's a useful distinction.
This feels much closer to what we're actually trying to achieve.

@46:18 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
I don't think we'd want to jump straight into solutions today.
Our next step should really be understanding your existing audience data, previous campaign performance and business priorities.
Once we understand that properly, we'll prepare an Alignment Snapshot to make sure we've understood the opportunity before recommending anything.

@51:02 – Sarah Johnson
That sounds like a sensible approach.
We'll share our audience insights, previous campaign summaries and current priorities over the next week.

ACTION ITEMS
Nike
Share audience research.
Share previous campaign performance.
Share priority product categories.
Introduce regional marketing stakeholders.
TTA
Prepare Alignment Snapshot.
Develop initial creator strategy.
Recommend creator archetypes.
Prepare measurement framework.
Schedule strategic workshop.

alignment_tool_analysis.about_the_organisation: Nike Inc operates in Nigeria as a globally recognised sportswear and athletic footwear brand within the tech-enabled consumer fitness sector. The organisation enjoys strong brand awareness and aspirational appeal across Nigerian markets, particularly for its running category products. Despite widespread recognition and fashion-driven purchase behaviour, the brand faces a strategic challenge in converting brand admiration into active participation in running. The marketing team has identified a gap between consumer ownership of Nike products and actual engagement in organised fitness activities such as local running clubs, weekend fitness groups, and structured running events. Previous influencer-led campaigns have delivered strong media metrics including reach, engagement, video views, and traffic during campaign windows, but have not sustained momentum or built lasting communities around running participation. The brand is now exploring a shift from traditional advertising approaches toward community-building strategies that address behaviour change rather than awareness. This reorientation reflects a recognition that Nigerian audiences require locally authentic engagement rather than imported campaign models, and that participation in running as a lifestyle behaviour requires different metrics and creator partnerships than product promotion alone.
alignment_tool_analysis.core_focus_areas: The organisation is focused on growing participation in running across Nigeria, moving beyond brand awareness to drive actual behaviour change among consumers who already know and admire the brand. The marketing leadership is investigating how creator-led community strategies can transition consumers from product ownership to active running participation. This includes examining the distinction between media-optimised influencer campaigns and community-centred creator partnerships that foster identity and belonging around running. The brand is also prioritising authenticity and local resonance over globalised campaign templates, acknowledging that Nigerian audiences require engagement strategies that feel genuinely created for them rather than simply localised.
alignment_tool_analysis.key_customers_beneficiaries: The primary audience comprises Nigerian consumers who currently purchase Nike products for fashion reasons but have not yet adopted running as a regular behaviour or lifestyle practice. This audience demonstrates strong brand affinity and ownership intent but shows limited participation in organised running activities, local running clubs, or weekend fitness groups. The brand recognises that these consumers require social permission and community invitation to transition from product buyers to active runners. The marketing team has observed that this audience responds differently to imported campaign models and requires locally authentic engagement to reduce emotional barriers to participation in running.
alignment_tool_analysis.key_goals_metrics: The organisation's central objective is to increase participation in running as a measurable behaviour rather than optimising traditional media metrics. Historically, the brand has evaluated campaigns primarily through reach, engagement, video views, traffic, and sales during campaign windows, but acknowledges it lacks a structured framework to measure participation itself. The marketing team is now seeking to establish metrics around community formation, sustained momentum beyond campaign periods, and ongoing engagement in running clubs, fitness groups, and organised running events. Success will be measured by whether consumers transition from admiring the brand to consistently putting on running shoes and identifying as runners within community structures.
alignment_tool_analysis.success_timeline: The organisation is approaching this strategic shift as a foundational reorientation rather than a short-term campaign, acknowledging that behaviour change requires ecosystem development rather than discrete activation windows. The brand has committed to sharing audience research, previous campaign performance data, and current priorities to inform strategy development. The marketing leadership recognises that sustaining momentum beyond traditional campaign cycles has been a previous weakness and that building communities around running participation will require longer-term investment in creator partnerships, running clubs, weekly participation structures, and community identity development rather than burst-based media spending.
alignment_tool_analysis.focus: The brand's strategic focus centres on reframing its marketing challenge from an awareness problem to a behaviour change problem, recognising that consumers already know Nike but require trusted communities and social permission to become active runners. The organisation is investigating how creators can function as community builders rather than content distributors, making running socially desirable and reducing emotional barriers to participation. This includes exploring the distinction between celebrity partnerships that generate attention and community creators who drive participation, with an expectation that community-layer creators will carry greater weight if behaviour change is the true objective. The marketing team is also examining how to design ecosystems that integrate running clubs, creator stories, music, weekly participation structures, challenges, digital content, and community identity rather than isolated campaign assets.
alignment_tool_analysis.priority: The organisation's immediate priority is to understand the full scope of its existing audience data, previous campaign performance across media and behavioural dimensions, and internal business priorities before committing to strategic recommendations. The brand has identified a need to develop new measurement frameworks that capture participation rather than impressions, and to establish creator partnership models that prioritise authenticity and community formation over reach optimisation. The marketing leadership is also prioritising the development of locally authentic engagement strategies that feel genuinely Nigerian rather than adapted from global templates, acknowledging that this authenticity is a critical predictor of success for creator-led campaigns. The team is preparing to introduce regional marketing stakeholders and receive strategic recommendations including creator archetypes, initial creator strategy, and measurement frameworks that align with behaviour change objectives.

--- Session 1 | 2026-09-09 ---
Nike x TTA: Exploring Creator-Led Growth for Nike Running - March 12
VIEW RECORDING – 58 mins (No highlights)

@0:00 – Sarah Johnson (Nike Marketing Director)
Jude, thank you for making the time. We've been following some of the work you've been doing around creator communities and behaviour change, and we thought this would be a good opportunity to exchange ideas.
To give a little context, we're currently looking closely at how we grow participation in running across Nigeria.
Nike is already a very well-known brand here, but awareness isn't really our challenge anymore.
The bigger question for us is how we move people from admiring the brand to actually putting on running shoes and becoming runners.
That's really the conversation we'd like to have today.

@1:38 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's really interesting because I actually think you've just described a behaviour problem rather than a marketing problem.
People already know Nike.
They probably even aspire to own Nike.
But becoming a runner is something completely different.
From our perspective, behaviour usually changes through trusted communities much faster than it changes through advertising.
So I don't think the question becomes "How do we advertise running?"
I think the question becomes "Who already has permission to influence that behaviour?"

@3:02 – Michael Adeyemi (Nike Brand Manager)
Exactly.
One thing we've observed is that many people buy Nike because it's fashionable.
But when we look at participation in organised runs, local running clubs or even weekend fitness groups, the numbers are still relatively small.
We think there's an opportunity there.
We've experimented with influencer campaigns before.
They've generated reach.
They've generated engagement.
But they haven't necessarily built communities.

@5:11 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Can I ask something?
When you evaluate those influencer campaigns internally, are you primarily measuring media metrics?
Or are you measuring behaviour?
Because those are very different things.
If you're looking at impressions, influencers perform one role.
If you're trying to create identity and belonging, the strategy changes completely.

@6:25 – Ada Obi (Nike Digital Marketing Lead)
Mostly media metrics.
Reach.
Engagement.
Video views.
Traffic.
Sales during campaign windows.
We've never really had a structured way to measure participation itself.

@7:42 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's helpful.
One thing we've learned is that creators become much more valuable when they're responsible for building communities rather than distributing content.
Someone doesn't wake up and become a runner because they watched one video.
They become runners because someone invited them into a community where running became normal.

@10:18 – Sarah Johnson
That's actually one of the reasons we're interested in this conversation.
We've started asking ourselves whether we should think less like advertisers and more like community builders.

@12:05 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
I think that's exactly where creators become strategic partners.
The creator isn't simply promoting the shoe.
They're making the behaviour socially desirable.
They're reducing the emotional barriers to participation.

@15:14 – Michael Adeyemi
One thing we'd like to avoid is another campaign that feels imported.
We've got incredible global assets, but Nigerian audiences respond differently.
We need something that genuinely feels local.

@17:20 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
That's actually encouraging to hear because authenticity is probably the biggest predictor of success for creator-led campaigns.
People can tell almost immediately when something has simply been localized versus genuinely created for them.

@21:11 – Sarah Johnson
Another question we'd love your thoughts on.
Should we work with celebrities?
Or should we work with smaller creators who already run communities?

@22:35 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Personally...
I don't think that's an either-or question.
Celebrities create attention.
Community creators create participation.
If the objective is behaviour change, I'd expect the community layer to carry much more weight.

@28:42 – Ada Obi
That's interesting because internally we've tended to optimise for reach.
Maybe that's why we've struggled to sustain momentum after campaigns finish.

@33:15 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
Exactly.
What we're really designing isn't a campaign.
We're designing an ecosystem.
Running clubs.
Creator stories.
Music.
Weekly participation.
Challenges.
Digital content.
Community identity.
The content becomes evidence that the community exists—not the other way around.

@41:56 – Sarah Johnson
I think that's a useful distinction.
This feels much closer to what we're actually trying to achieve.

@46:18 – Jude Abaga (TTA)
I don't think we'd want to jump straight into solutions today.
Our next step should really be understanding your existing audience data, previous campaign performance and business priorities.
Once we understand that properly, we'll prepare an Alignment Snapshot to make sure we've understood the opportunity before recommending anything.

@51:02 – Sarah Johnson
That sounds like a sensible approach.
We'll share our audience insights, previous campaign summaries and current priorities over the next week.

--- Transcript ---
Summary:

The team decided to prioritize the B2C consumer wallet and set growth targets for initial rollout.
• Prioritize B2C consumer wallet launch
• Target 100,000 new users per quarter
• Defer cooperatives to phase two
• Jude committed campaign concepts and budgets

alignment_snapshot_fields.about_the_organisation: Parkway is a financial technology company operating in Nigeria's fintech sector, delivering a suite of products across consumer and institutional segments. The organisation's primary offering is a consumer wallet product that provides virtual card functionality, enabling users to manage subscriptions (including services such as Google and Canva), participate in cooperative savings arrangements, and conduct digital transactions. Beyond the consumer wallet, Parkway operates in hospital-linked payment collection through a sister company that secures government contracts at state level, though this institutional segment functions as a closed loop requiring minimal marketing intervention. The brand also maintains a cooperative-focused product line earmarked for future rollout. Parkway's leadership has identified the consumer wallet as the immediate growth driver requiring marketing support, reflecting a strategic choice to concentrate resources on the B2C segment before expanding to cooperatives. The organisation is positioning its wallet as an everyday financial utility with broad household penetration ambitions, distinguished by its virtual card capabilities in a market where digital payment infrastructure continues to mature. Parkway's current commercial context centres on user acquisition velocity in a competitive consumer fintech landscape, with the team demonstrating a disciplined approach to segment prioritisation rather than pursuing multiple verticals simultaneously.
alignment_snapshot_fields.core_focus_areas: The immediate focus area is the consumer wallet product, which the organisation has designated as the first-phase marketing priority. The wallet's virtual card feature represents a core value proposition, supporting subscription payments and cooperative participation use cases. The leadership team has explicitly deprioritised hospital payment collection activities because these operate through a sister company managing government negotiations and state contracts, effectively functioning as a closed-loop business requiring no external marketing. Cooperatives have been identified as a second-phase opportunity once the consumer wallet achieves traction. The organisation is concentrating on broad consumer adoption of the wallet product, with the stated ambition to place the wallet in the hands of every potential user, signalling mass-market intent rather than niche positioning.
alignment_snapshot_fields.key_customers_beneficiaries: The primary customer segment is B2C consumers who require digital wallet services for everyday financial transactions, subscription management, and participation in cooperative savings structures. The consumer base includes individuals using the wallet for recurring digital service payments such as streaming platforms, productivity tools, and other subscription-based services that accept virtual card payments. The wallet also serves consumers seeking to enhance their financial participation through cooperative membership, suggesting an audience interested in both transactional convenience and structured savings. The hospital payment collection segment, while part of Parkway's broader ecosystem, targets institutional clients through a separate sister company and does not represent a marketing-driven customer base. The phased approach to cooperatives indicates a secondary audience of group savings participants and cooperative administrators who will become priority customers once the initial consumer wallet rollout demonstrates market validation.
alignment_snapshot_fields.key_goals_metrics: The organisation has set a quantified user acquisition target of 100,000 additional B2C wallet users per quarter, serving as the primary success metric for the consumer wallet initiative. This quarterly benchmark translates to a pro-rated expectation of 200,000 new users before year-end, acknowledging the engagement is beginning partway through the third quarter. The leadership team confirmed this growth target represents significant and desirable performance, using it as the planning baseline for campaign development. Success is measured through net new user additions rather than transaction volume, wallet balances, or revenue metrics in the available conversation, indicating that initial growth strategy prioritises user base expansion and market penetration velocity. The team referenced these targets as captured documentation reviewed during the engagement, with unanimous affirmation that achieving the stated volume would constitute meaningful commercial progress for the business.
alignment_snapshot_fields.success_timeline: The organisation is operating on a phased rollout timeline beginning with the consumer wallet as the immediate priority, followed by cooperatives in a subsequent phase. The engagement conversation occurred during the third quarter of the calendar year, with pro-rated user acquisition targets applied from that point through year-end. A follow-up milestone was scheduled for mid-August to review campaign concepts and budget recommendations, establishing a rhythm of iterative planning and execution rather than a single campaign launch. The phased approach defers cooperative segment marketing until the wallet achieves traction, though no explicit timeline for phase two transition was stated. The team emphasised flexibility in working models that can be adjusted as campaigns progress, suggesting an adaptive timeline responsive to performance data rather than fixed long-range commitments.
alignment_snapshot_fields.focus: Parkway's marketing focus centres entirely on driving consumer adoption of the wallet product through a concentrated B2C acquisition campaign. The organisation has made an explicit strategic decision to narrow from multiple potential segments to a single priority, resisting the temptation to market across hospital collections, cooperatives, and wallet offerings simultaneously. This discipline reflects leadership experience that younger companies often dilute impact by pursuing too many initiatives concurrently. The wallet's value proposition emphasises everyday utility through virtual card functionality, positioning the product as essential infrastructure for digital subscription management rather than a novelty financial tool. The marketing agenda is to establish the wallet as ubiquitous consumer technology, with cooperatives and other segments deliberately held in reserve until the primary offering demonstrates market validation and sustainable growth.
alignment_snapshot_fields.priority: The overriding priority is executing a B2C consumer wallet acquisition campaign capable of delivering 100,000 net new users per quarter, supported by creative concepts and budget allocations to be developed in the immediate engagement phase. Campaign development takes precedence over segment expansion, with the organisation explicitly deferring cooperative marketing and requiring no hospital collection support due to the closed-loop structure of that business line. The team prioritised clarity and focus, welcoming the recommendation to concentrate resources rather than fragment efforts across multiple audiences. Budget recommendations and pitch ideas represent the next critical deliverable, with approval contingent on the creative direction hitting strategic targets. The leadership team values over-planning relative to under-resourcing, indicating a priority on ambitious rather than conservative campaign scoping during the planning phase.
